## Sleep deprivation and performance

A 2003 paper by Belenky *et al.* investigates the impact of sleep deprivation on reaction time.  18 volunteers in the study were restricted to 3 hours of time in bed each night, and were monitored over the course of 10 nights. After each night, they were asked to perform a task in which they reacted to a visual stimulus (pressing a button as quickly as possible after the visual stimulus appeared).

The data consist of 180 observations (10 nights for each of the 18 participants), with the following variables:

* `Reaction`: reaction time in the task (ms)
* `Days`: day of the study (number of days of sleep deprivation)
* `Subject`: the subject ID

\bigskip

**Question:** Propose a model that the researchers could use to investigate the effect of sleep deprivation on reaction time.

## Chemistry A-level scores

In Britain, A-levels are exams taken by students before attending university. Unlike in the US, British students specialize in a subset of subjects in the last few years of their high school studies, and A-levels are national exams assessing their mastery of their chosen subjects. Good scores on A-levels are necessary to pursue the corresponding degrees at university level.

We have data on scores for 31022 students taking the A-level chemistry exam in Britain, from 2280 different schools. Additionally, each school belongs to a Local Education Authority: there are 131 such authorities in the data. 

The data contain 31022 rows, and the following columns:

* `lea`: Local Education Authority identifier
* `school`: School identifier
* `student`: Student identifier
* `score`: score on the A-level Chemistry exam
* `gcse`: score on the GCSE exam (this is an earlier exam that students take halfway through high school, before beginning their A-level studies)

\bigskip

**Question:** Propose a model that the researchers could use to model student scores on the A-level chemistry exam.
